topic: Latter-day Saint hymns and hymnbook history: historical editions through 1989
method: Fixed, editorially paraphrased source pack from official Church sources. Historical events and beliefs are represented as documented in those sources. No live retrieval or model-written fact sheets. This is a grounded multistage comparison, not a memory or retrieval benchmark.

sections.title: The First Hymnbooks
sections.body: A July 1830 revelation now in Doctrine and Covenants 25 directed Emma Smith to select hymns. William W. Phelps helped prepare her first collection. Its title page says 1835, but printing finished in early 1836 in Kirtland. It contained 90 hymns and no musical notation. Hymns appeared in The Evening and the Morning Star in 1832. Emma’s second collection was printed in Nauvoo in 1841 and contained 304 hymns. An influential British collection appeared in Manchester in 1840 under Brigham Young, Parley P. Pratt, and John Taylor. Do not conflate title-page year with completion of printing.

sections.title: Who Wrote the Words?
sections.body: Text authors, not composers: William W. Phelps wrote Praise to the Man and The Spirit of God. Eliza R. Snow wrote O My Father and Though Deepening Trials. Parley P. Pratt wrote The Morning Breaks and Truth Eternal. George Manwaring wrote Joseph Smith’s First Prayer. William Fowler wrote We Thank Thee, O God, for a Prophet. John Nicholson wrote Come, Follow Me. William Clayton wrote Come, Come, Ye Saints. Samuel Medley wrote I Know That My Redeemer Lives. These credits refer to the English hymns as included in the 1985 hymnbook.

sections.title: Who Wrote the Music?
sections.body: For these English settings in the 1985 hymnbook, George Careless composed The Morning Breaks; Alexander Schreiner composed Truth Eternal; James McGranahan composed the music used for O My Father; and Ebenezer Beesley composed High on the Mountain Top. The music credit for Joseph Smith’s First Prayer names Sylvanus Billings Pond, adapted by A. C. Smyth. Caroline Sheridan Norton composed the music used for We Thank Thee, O God, for a Prophet. Samuel McBurney composed Come, Follow Me. Lowell Mason composed the setting of Nearer, My God, to Thee. Distinguish an original composer from an adapter and a text author.

sections.title: Songs of the Pioneers
sections.body: William Clayton wrote the words to Come, Come, Ye Saints on April 15, 1846, while camped in Iowa. News that his wife Diantha had delivered a healthy baby boy prompted the writing. The Church’s museum pairs this manuscript with Eliza R. Snow’s Hail to the Twelve, and Pioneers, written in September 1847. Joel H. Johnson wrote High on the Mountain Top in 1853, drawing inspiration from Isaiah. Ebenezer Beesley composed that hymn’s music. In the 1985 English hymnbook, the standard congregational setting of Come, Come, Ye Saints is number 30, distinct from the men’s choir setting at number 326.

sections.title: Shared Christian Hymn Heritage
sections.body: The 1985 English hymnbook includes these hymns with roots in the wider Christian tradition: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God credits Martin Luther for its text. Abide with Me! credits Henry F. Lyte for its text; it is a different hymn from Abide with Me; ’Tis Eventide. Lead, Kindly Light has words by John Henry Newman and music by John B. Dykes. Nearer, My God, to Thee has words by Sarah F. Adams and music by Lowell Mason. All Creatures of Our God and King draws on Saint Francis of Assisi and uses a musical arrangement by Ralph Vaughan Williams.

sections.title: Later Hymnbook Milestones
sections.body: Latter-Day Saints’ Psalmody, issued in 1889, was the first large collection of Church hymns with musical notation. The Northern States Mission in Chicago published Songs of Zion beginning in 1908. A Church Music Committee was formed in 1920. Latter-Day Saint Hymns appeared in 1927, followed by a revised Hymns volume in 1948. The English 1985 hymnbook contains 341 hymns, including 92 then-new selections and 26 also found in Emma Smith’s original collection. Children’s Songbook was first published in 1989. These facts describe those historical editions, not the contents or publication status of the newer Hymns—For Home and Church.
